ch07.note: The Kwantung Army (関東軍), the Imperial Japanese Army's garrison in the Kwantung Leased Territory and, after 1931, in occupied Manchuria. Fiercely autonomous, it engineered the 1931 seizure of the Northeast and the founding of Manchukuo, and it was the driving force behind Japan's push into North China throughout this book.

ch07.anchor: Northern Expedition of the National Revolutionary Army
ch07.note: The Northern Expedition (1926–28), the military campaign by which Chiang Kai-shek's National Revolutionary Army marched north from Guangzhou, broke the great warlords one by one, and brought most of China under a single Nationalist government at Nanjing. It is the event that made the Republic Chen served.

'Rivers and lakes' (江湖, jianghu) names the floating world outside settled society—wandering knights, outlaws, gangsters, martial-arts men, fortune-tellers, and drifters, with its own code and slang. To be 'of the rivers and lakes' is to belong to that itinerant underworld.

From the Dao De Jing: 'Heaven's net is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing slips through' (天网恢恢，疏而不失)—the wicked may seem to escape, but justice, sooner or later, catches all. Chen invokes it over the fated end of his quarry.

ch07.anchor: bamboo already formed in his breast
ch07.note: The idiom xiong you cheng zhu (胸有成竹), 'the finished bamboo already in the breast,' from Su Shi's account of the painter Wen Tong, who saw the whole plant complete in his mind before setting brush to silk: to act with a fully formed plan already in hand.

A folk saying: goldthread (黄连, the root Coptis) is proverbially the bitterest of medicines, so 'a mute eating goldthread' can taste the bitterness but cannot voice it—one who must swallow a hardship in silence, unable to complain.

ch07.anchor: never laid down the butcher's knife
ch07.note: An inversion of the Buddhist saying 'lay down the butcher's knife and become a Buddha on the spot' (放下屠刀，立地成佛)—that even a killer may attain enlightenment the moment he repents. Chen's jibe is that this pious warlord kept the knife to the last and never truly repented.

A pailou (牌楼), a freestanding ornamental gateway of wood or stone straddling a street or marking an approach, often raised to honor a person or event. Beijing districts such as 'Dongsi Pailou' ('East Four Archways') took their names from them.
The traditional courtesy of greeting or thanks (作揖 / 拱手): one cups a fist in the other hand before the chest and inclines the body, the everyday polite gesture of old China in place of a handshake.

Licensed courtesans were entered on an official roll; to 'redeem' one (从良, congliang, 'return to the respectable') meant paying the house a large sum to strike her from that register and buy her out of her indenture, usually to take her as a wife or concubine.
